utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber where all the names of the establishment duties and the ranks are listed that refer to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: They are under item 3 and 4, where it is stated precisely at what level of the unit the person commanded and what their establishment rank was, based on which their retirement pension calculation was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: According to this regulation, could anybody receive early retirement by the head or minister of the HVO Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: According to this regulation, they're not listed, so they could not achieve their right to early retirement.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Let us look at the last document, and that is 2D01183. Would you please explain to the Trial Chamber what this law has to do with this previous regulation that we looked at?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: This is the Law on Special Rights of Recipients of War Decorations and Awards and Their Family Members, and it provides for the decorations that are included in these rights, and they would be receiving remuneration, up to 50 per cent of the average salary in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So those who were given these awards and decorations would have a right to that, as well as they secured their rights pursuant to the previous regulation that we looked at, the right to retirement.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please clarify for the Trial Chamber, even though this is obvious, when was this law adopted and who adopted it? And this is on the last page.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: This law was suggested by the Government of the Federation, and it was adopted by the Government and the Council of the Federation, and it lists the awards on the basis of which these rights can be granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And in which article is this referred to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: This is mentioned in Article 2 of this law.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm just going to remind you that in the document 2D1182, Article 1, referring to decorations and the declaration or the regulation on beneficial retirement, is referred to also in Article 5, so could you please look at Article 5 now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Are these decorations listed here, and can you please explain to the Trial Chamber what this means? There are two tables here. Can you explain them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: The decorations are listed here which were given to members of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Army, this is the first column, and the second column are decorations given to members of the Croatian Defence Council. And based on that, they secured their right to a supplemental monthly income.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now we're talking about document 2D1183 in the e-court collection. Let us please wait until that appears on your screen, 1183, Article 5. There is the Order of the Croatian Tree Foil, the Order of Ban Jelacic, the Order of Nikolas Subic Zrinski, the Order of Prince Domagoj With Necklace. Who would receive these decorations? Who awarded these decorations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: They were awarded by the Republic of Croatia to members of HVO forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And those listed on the left-hand side, that would be the Order of Freedom, the Golden Lily Badge, who was awarded these decorations -- who awarded them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: This was awarded by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Pinjuh, does that mean that the right to this benefit, retirement, was granted under the same conditions both to members of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Army and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, they were granted this right under equal conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And, finally, you, as a member of the association that you referred to earlier, do you know if members of the HVO and the Bosnia-Herzegovina Army were granted the right according to this decree?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, they have been granted and have secured this right. Those who were awarded these decorations are receiving these pensions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Other than these who received the decorations, is the retirement benefit granted to persons in the military hierarchy in the positions that we saw in the document 2D1180?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, they also have been granted this right to military pension.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you this: I was given information that on page 48, line 6, in the transcript the word is missing "Bosnia and Herzegovina Army."

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: No, you don't have to worry about that. That was your answer or, rather, my question. I asked you if the -- both members of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Army and the HVO had the same right. In line 6, we are missing the word "Army." Witness, thank you very much for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have finished my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a follow-up question for you on the law and decree we have just seen. I discover the existence of this text today, unfortunately. Had I been made aware of it beforehand, I could have put questions who came to testify before you, people who were involved in the political life of the country, but this is not the case, and we are faced with these documents at the last minute. This is why I'm putting this question to you. I don't know whether you will be able to answer this question. I hope you can, because you told us a while ago that you had been the secretary of an association of people who got together to defend their rights to a pension after the war. Therefore, in this capacity I believe you have some understanding of these matters. By looking at the law which was adopted in Parliament, which is on document 2D1183, in Article 1 it is said that this applies to people that have died or who are missing, members of the BiH and members of the HVO also, for their role as servicemen between the 18th of September 1991 and the 23rd of December 1995. Did you attend these Assembly sessions when these were discussed in Parliament or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, this law was discussed in Parliament and was adopted in both chambers of the Federation Assembly or Parliament.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you follow what was going on in Parliament?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not engaged in any way in reference to this law on military decorations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you had followed what was going on in Parliament, well, then we would have had this on the transcript. We had as an exhibit a decision by the Constitutional Court, who declared the HVO illegal. It would be interesting to see what this decision contained, since the HVO had been declared illegal, since the HVO had played a part in defending the country. So this was probably addressed in Parliament. It would have been interesting to get an insight into this. But since you didn't follow this, you are unable to answer. We may be able to elicit answers from other witnesses who will come at a later stage. Now, this is my last question. You, yourself, did you receive a pension? Because you had been an HVO fighter in Sarajevo for some time, you may have received a decoration. I don't know. Whatever the case may be, are you currently receiving a pension or will you receive a pension?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... retired on the basis of the decoration, the Order of the Croatian Tree Foil.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are getting a pension because you were a combatant and part of the HVO and a member of the Croatian Clover, the Order of the Clover. So I shall now put the question to other Defence counsel. Mr. Coric's Defence counsel. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, it's been a while now since we've heard you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. I believe I did speak yesterday, or said a couple of words, at least. We have no questions for the gentleman, but we do wish to thank him for coming here to give his evidence. And we wish him good luck and safe travels. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. The Defence of General Praljak also does not consider it necessary to question this witness, and I would also like to thank the witness for coming here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of General Petkovic does consider it necessary to put some questions to this witness, because I believe that we have an exceptionally rare situation to hear somebody who was in Sarajevo during the war, and who cooperated with the Bosnia and Herzegovina Army, and who can provide some relevant information to us about the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. My questions are going to deal with the clarification of two statements by the witness. Another topic will be the attack of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the MUP on the HVO Brigade in Sarajevo. And the third topic, if there is time, will deal with some regulations about the defence in Bosnia and Herzegovina to see at what age somebody could be engaged in the army, and some other issues pertaining to the Law on National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pinjuh, my name is Vesna Alaburic, I'm an attorney from Zagreb, and in these proceedings I am defending General Milivoj Petkovic, and I would like you to clarify one of your statements, as it seemed very, very important to me. When you spoke about your second exit from Sarajevo or departure from Sarajevo, and when you mentioned that you were stopped at check-points near Konjic and Jablanica, you said how mostly you were surprised because the check-points were in the free territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The statement was recorded on page 21. Can you please tell us, Mr. Pinjuh, whether these were Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina check-points?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you meant in the area that was under the control of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was considered free territory, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also mentioned today how, for you, it was not in dispute that the HVO was a component part or an ally in the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was on pages 30 to 31 of the transcript. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, you understood me correctly. I was convinced that we were an integral part of the forces of -- the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My colleague showed you a decree earlier. You don't need to look for it. I'm going to tell you, on the basis of the transcript, what document this is. 2D1181. And in that document, Mr. Pinjuh, it says that the decree refers to, I quote: "Members of the former Army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (the Croatian Defence Council) and the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Mr. Pinjuh, can you please tell us, according to what you know, was there ever any dilemma that the HVO and the Bosnia and Herzegovina Army were equal components of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: In all the regulations, they are treated as equal.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Earlier, His Honour Judge Antonetti put a question to you about a decision of the Constitutional Court, this is page 50 of today's transcript, which allegedly proclaimed the HVO as an illegal organisation, and His Honour Judge Antonetti asked how come that members of the HVO were granted certain rights. I'm going to ask you to clarify this Constitutional Court decision of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If you know, did this decision refer to the constituting the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna so that the Constitution would then say that that decision on the Constitution of the HZ-HB was illegal?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: I really don't know anything about that document. I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina ever adopted any decision under which the HVO, as an organisation, either a civilian or a military organisation, would be declared an illegal one?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: I don't know when the Constitutional Court adopted that decision, I really don't know, but I know that the lines that we held in Sarajevo in 1992 and 1993 we were holding with the agreement -- I mean, we were entrusted with guarding a certain part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Witness, in my set of documents, and I'm going to begin with document 3 in that set, and this is number 4D1266 -- take a look at that document, please, because I am following on from the examination-in-chief, in which you said, Mr. Pinjuh, that in August 1993, you talked to the commander, Mr. Zelic -- yes, Zelic, and he told you that the BH Army wanted to disband the HVO Brigade in Sarajevo. And also we saw a document, 2D1193 was its number, in which at the end of -- at the beginning of October, Mr. Boban, among other things, speaks about the danger of abolishing the HVO Brigade. Now let's take a look at this document together. This comes from the Security Administration of the Supreme Command Staff of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it is dated the 26th of September, 1993. It is signed by the chief, Jusuf Jasarevic. To start off with, please, Mr. Pinjuh, tell me whether you knew the Supreme Command Staff of the BH Army and that it had a Security Administration?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And is this name familiar, Jusuf Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, did you have any knowledge of information at all to the effect that the Sarajevo Brigade would be the subject of special interest and processing by the Security Administration of the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: I think that they did that continuously. They had intelligence surveillance of our units on a continuous basis, and I think that they took our members, the members of units, for interviews as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, in that document, let's look at page 2, and I'd like to draw your attention there to a particular section at the end of the first paragraph. The Security Administration notes that the irresponsible relationship and attitude of the HVO soldiers to defence tasks on the right bank of the Miljacka River, failure to carry out guard duty at night, allowing the Serbs to pass through, and so on and so forth, that is what is referred to. Now, tell me, Mr. Pinjuh, you told us that the HVO Brigade in Sarajevo performed all its tasks and responsibilities in the defence of Sarajevo in the most professional manner. Do you stand by that state, despite what the Security Administration says here about HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: I stand by what I said, that the HVO defended the line professionally and did so successfully.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Now look at the next document, 4D1500 is the number, and it is an order by the commander of the Main Staff, Rasim Delic, dated the 28th of October, in which, in point 1 it says: "Disband the HVO Main Staff of the City of Sarajevo with the headquarter support units and all HVO municipal staffs established on the municipality of the city of Sarajevo." And then under number 2, it says: "The former Kralj Tvrtko HVO Brigade is formed from the territories of...," and I shall skip that part, "shall be renamed and recorded from now on under the name of the Kralj Tvrtko Croatian Brigade." And then they go on to say that this Kralj Tvrtko Croatian Brigade is hereby placed under direct command of the BH Army 1st Corps. And in point 4, it says that these tasks should be implemented immediately. And under point 2 of Chapter 4, it says that the Croatian Brigade should be entered in the schedule of the basic mobilisation plan of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the 1st Corps section, straight away. Now, having seen this order, Mr. Pinjuh, can you tell us whether that was the order by the commander of the BH Army stating that an attack should be launched on the HVO Brigade in Sarajevo, to have that brigade disbanded and renamed into a Croatian brigade and put under the 1st Corps of the BH Army establishment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: From this order, yes, we could say that that was their intention.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at the next document, which is 4D1714, and that's the last document in my set. Once again, the Security Administration of the Supreme Command Staff of the BH Army. It is dated the 25th of November, 1993, and here we have an analysis of what has been achieved, what was done. Let's try and focus on some points that I consider to be most significant, because it's rather a long document and we don't have time to go through the whole of it. Anyway, in the introduction, it says that: "The associate forces of our army and the MUP carried out a blockade of the HVO Main Staff and units, and parts of the defence lines in Sarajevo that were held by members of the HVO Kralj Tvrtko Brigade." Tell me, please, Mr. Pinjuh, is that precisely what you described earlier on, whereby the special MUP units and the BH Army attacked HVO units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, those were my -- that was my information.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now we come to the next observation made. After all the plan measures were implemented to disband the Main Staff --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Alaburic. This may be again a linguistic point. In this report, I read the words "carried out a blockade on the HVO Main Staff and units, and parts of the defence line." You have used the word "attack." Is it one and the same word in Croatian? If not, it might be interesting to know the difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can tell you my thoughts on those words now, and concepts, and perhaps Mr. Praljak, as a well-known linguist, could explain this better. But let me tell you of my understanding of this. An attack can be launched in different ways. You can carry out an attack in different ways. You can carry out an attack by blocking someone in a facility or feature, or at a certain position, and then make it impossible for that other party to act in any way, and then as that party surrenders, you disarm them, and then go ahead that way. Now, in my opinion, what happened in Sarajevo was that kind of attack. Of course, there can be other types of attack with shooting and more aggressive taking control of a territory, if the party wish to block -- puts up resistance. Now, as the witness said there was no armed resistance, that means that this type of attack, which is called here a blockade, was put in place, and the BH Army and the MUP units achieved their goal that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pinjuh, can you confirm this? Is this the way you understood it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's how I understood it. And I think that the Geneva Conventions were violated on captured members of the other side, where they were beaten, taken into detention, as expressed in these reports, and everything took place on the day when the blockade was put in place; and the leadership of the HVO, President Zelic was arrested, so was Commander Vulic, and part of the leadership was -- were also arrested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We've had that. As I'm concerned, you can continue, Ms. Alaburic, but I don't know whether the President wants --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Witness, it may be more complicated than you think. I'm sure that you don't have all the material available to you. You call this an attack, but there could be another aspect to it. Did you know that there was an international conference being held in Geneva, aiming at finding solutions to all these problems? Did you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You didn't know, for instance, that as part of that work, it was envisioned that, say, HVO units would be incorporated into the ABiH and that ABiH units would be incorporated into the HVO? Did you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise, but can we clarify one point here? The Vance-Owen Plan was not to integrate them, that is to say, the HVO units in certain areas into the BH Army and vice versa, but to resubordinate them, so for something to happen which actually did occur in Sarajevo throughout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. One last question. Did you know, sir, that Mr. Prlic sent a letter to Mr. Izetbegovic along those lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not know Mr. Prlic, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You did not know. Very well. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, let's see what the Security Administration goes on to say further on, and the next sentence in that same paragraph is this: "After that, all planned measures were carried out to disband the HVO Main Staff and to transform its existing brigades into the Croatian Kralj Tvrtko Brigade under the command of the 1st Corps." Tell us, please, Mr. Pinjuh, is that precisely what happened, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes. The brigade was established later on, the Kralj Tvrtko Brigade, and it was under the command of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And now the next sentence reads as follows: "A staff of this brigade was created and a commander appointed, and the appointment of other commanders is ongoing, as well as the take-over of defence lines held by the former HVO." Tell us, please, Mr. Pinjuh, to the best of your knowledge, does that correspond to what the realistic situation was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: I think that when they established the brigade, it did carry out the orders of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in paragraph 2, roughly the middle of the second paragraph, it says as follows, that: "Seven members of the Main Staff of the HVO were arrested in Sarajevo," and I'm going to mention their names, which are mentioned in brackets: Slavko Zelic, Ivan Vulic -- Ivan Vulic, V-u-l-i-c, V for Victoria, u-l-i-v, Tomislav Kokar, K-o-k-a-r.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Kokar, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, Vinko Bosnjak, Zeljko Jukic -- Vinko Bosnjak, Zeljko Jukic, and Zeljko Maric. Now, tell us, Mr. Pinjuh, to the best of your knowledge, were those indeed the commanders of the HVO Brigade in Sarajevo who were arrested?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Ivan Vulic was the brigade commander. Tomislav Kokar was the assistant for security. Vinko Bosnjak was the chief, and Slavko Zelic was the president, and Zeljko Jukic was the deputy president of the HVO in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, it goes on to say that a criminal report was filed against Slavko Zelic and that the other persons expressed the obligatory loyalty to the BH Army and were included into the newly-formed Croatian Kralj Tvrtko Brigade through the appropriate operative measures. Now, tell us, is that true, was a criminal report filed against Mr. Slavko Zelic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: I think so, yes, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. So you don't know what happened next, do you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: I think that Ivan Vulic, as brigade commander, was never engaged in the newly established brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Thank you for those answers, Mr. Pinjuh. And now I would like to ask you, as somebody who was in Sarajevo and closely cooperated with the BH Army there, to try and help me understand some documents better, and these documents are already exhibits, they've already been admitted into evidence, but I think it would be an important thing for the Judges to see them. The first document is 4D409, and that is a decree law on the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Pinjuh. Can you help us to understand Article 2 of that decree law better? And this is how it reads: "The Republic's armed forces shall comprise of the Army of the Republic, herein after the Army. In the event of war, the Armed Forces shall be, in addition to the Army, the police and armed units which shall be placed under the united command of the Republic's armed forces." Paragraph 2: "The armed units described under para 1 herein shall be considered to be workers engaged in securing enterprises and other legal entities and the employees of the Customs Service and other frontier organs." My question to you, Mr. Pinjuh, is this: If we wish to define the status of the members of the armed forces of the BH Army, which in these proceedings can be of importance, that is to say, whether somebody has the status of a POW or not, then in a broad manner we should try to establish whether somebody was indeed a member of the armed forces or not. So am I interpreting this correctly, that this concept does not only refer to the soldiers of the BH Army, in the narrow sense of the word, but to all persons enumerated here as being members of the armed forces? If you can't comment on that article, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: I think this second paragraph relates to the persons who had a work obligation; that is to say, they weren't directly in the military units, but they had a work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So are you saying that work obligations were considered to be a contribution and part and parcel of the country's defence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll be able to see that in the next document, which is 4D408, which is a decree law on defence, the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'm going to ask you, Mr. Pinjuh, about some details. For example, in Article 5 of that decree, it says that the Republic, through its ministries and other Republican organs in the area of defence, in the realm of defence, directs the resistance of the people during wartime.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: I apologise, but I haven't found that yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. It's Article 5.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: What page is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It says page 5 of the Official Gazette, but look at the article, sir. It's Article 5, and the document number is 4D408, and it's on page 2. You'll find Article 5 on page 2, and it says: "Directs the resistance of the people in wartime." And I'm interested in that, the resistance of the people in wartime. Tell us, please, Mr. Pinjuh, does this provision have anything to do with the total national defence concept and social self-protection, as was in place in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if I can answer that question, how the Territorial Defence was organised. I'm not sure I know how to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I wasn't asking you about the Territorial Defence. I was asking you about the concept of total national defence and social self-protection, that concept.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Well, yes, that was a concept that was mentioned in the former Yugoslavia very frequently, and exercises and training courses were conducted, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That according to that concept, each citizen of the country, after a certain age, had a specific role in the defence of their country, they had special rights and duties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right, very well. Let us now look at Article 51. Let's see at what age did a person start having certain duties. It says here: "All citizens between 15 and 60, men, or 55, women, have the right and obligation to train for defence -- to attend training." Mr. Pinjuh, I'm interested here, at this age of 15. Did you know that was the age in Bosnia and Herzegovina at which a person could start being trained for the defence of the country?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In these proceedings, we very often had --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The last line on questioning from Counsel Alaburic, to the Prosecution, seems to be outside the scope of the direct examination, so we're asking for an explanation on that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, you are asking questions, and I fail to see the relevance of those questions. Maybe this is not the right witness for them. If you want to waste your time, you're free to do so, but I don't think this is the right witness for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you'll permit me an explanation. We have spent a lot of time in this courtroom discussing whether under-age persons were detained in Heliodrom, Dretelj, or in any of the prisons under the control of the HVO, and I think that this question, asking what happens with under-age persons and what their role was in the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, is one of the key questions in these proceedings. If you think differently, I am very sorry, but I really do consider this to be one of the main questions, and I believe that it is my task in these proceedings to prove that people of 15 did have certain duties in the defence in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I would like to say that up until 2000, this was totally in accordance with the International Convention on the Protection of Children in Times of War, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood you, and I'm going to show that I understood, because I'm going to ask the witness. Were they individuals aged 15 or 16 who were combatting with you in Sarajevo; 15, 16, or 17?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not accept under-age members in the brigade. We took care that we accepted only those as members who had served their military term of duty in the Army of Yugoslavia. Yes, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The remark from the Prosecution did go to the line of questioning being outside the scope of direct examination, so that was our concern, and I don't think that counsel has replied to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will see whether some time should be deducted from Ms. Alaburic's time and credited to the time for examination-in-chief. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, basically I have finished my cross-examination, in view of the fact that the witness said that he's not aware of these regulations about the age limits. I have no intention of putting him -- to him any questions about the armed forces of the -- of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. Pinjuh, I would like to thank you for your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One follow-up question. Let's go back to document 4D1266, drawn up by Jusuf Jasarevic. Sir, it's an ABiH document, isn't it, showing the views of the party that was the adversary of the HVO. Have you found the document? I'm interested in the second line there, where Mr. Jusuf mentions clashes between the HVO and the ABiH in Central Bosnia and in the Neretva Valley. When I saw that word "clashes," I asked myself what it meant precisely, because I don't know what word was used in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Okrsaj".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Okrsaj." I see. Does that mean skirmishes or conflict? From your point of view - we know that at some point in time you were in Sarajevo and then you left Sarajevo - the fighting between the HVO and the ABiH, was that "okrsaj" for you, just sort of every now and then some skirmishes and then there would be a lull, or did you have large-scale actions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the scale of the conflict was in the theatre in the different municipalities in Central Bosnia. As far as Herzegovina is concerned, I think that at the beginning of the conflict, lines were set up right at the start, and everybody was holding those lines until further notice, and then we had clashes at those lines. But I'm really not aware of the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I want to record on the transcript that an official ABiH document mentioned skirmishes. Let me move to the last document, 4D1714. Towards the middle of the document, earlier on Ms. Alaburic put a question to you, saying that there was a criminal report against Slavko Zelic for six alleged crimes, but she did not read the rest. It also appears that the three liaison officers were involved or were mentioned in the report, because the ABiH seems to incriminate Anton Rill for aiding the enemy. We've never seen Anton Rill. This is the first time we've heard about him. Was he that close to you that one could be led to believe that he was "collaborating" with the HVO, or was he neutral? Would he just report to his chain of command the information he would get? Why, in your view, is he being incriminated by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anton Rill was a liaison officer of the HVO with UNPROFOR, the HVO Sarajevo, so he set up cooperation between the UNPROFOR and the Croatian Defence Council in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why is he being incriminated by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that there was a lot of propaganda here and unfounded accusations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you think it's propaganda. Very well. Is the Prosecution ready to start with their cross-examination ?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: We're entirely in your hands, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you can start, and then we'll have a break at 12.30. Since you have two hours, we can continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like a clarification. Perhaps I didn't understand sufficiently, but I think that in the beginning you said that there would be enough time allocated for the cross-examination, the same amount of time that was allocated for the examination-in-chief. And so in view of the fact that I had used only one hour and fifteen minutes, does that mean that the Prosecution will have that same amount of time for the cross-examination or that original starting period of time that was allocated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Bench is going to discuss the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleagues would like the Prosecutor to state their views. Madam, here is the problem: Mr. Stojic's Defence had scheduled two hours. The Trial Chamber issued a decision granting two hours to the Stojic Defence and two hours to the OTP, but the Stojic Defence realised that two hours may be too much. It could be a waste of time that could be better used with other witnesses. Therefore, the Stojic Defence decided to shorten its time and use only one hour and fifteen minutes. Now, they say, "Well, if I used one hour and fifteen minutes, there's no reason why the Prosecution should have two hours." So that's the problem. What is your view?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution view is that the time we have been allocated is two hours for cross-examination, and we stand by that, but it might very well be that we will be able to finish in a shorter time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I didn't see you. You are at the back. Usually, you are a front-bench, but you are the last one in the classroom today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps relegated for naughty -- Your Honour, perhaps relegated for naughty behaviour. One never knows. But, Your Honour, in relation to this issue, it is my respectful submission that the spirit behind Your Honour's previous ruling, that there should be a symmetry between the time afforded for examination-in-chief and the time allocated for cross-examination, should be honoured, not only as an incentive for all parties to be diligent with the amount of time they use, and not to be wasteful or profligate with time, but also when one looks at the mischief. If the Defence have considered it appropriate to cut down examination-in-chief and restrict it to those matters that are most relevant in one hour and fifteen minutes, consistent with the spirit of Your Honour's clear decisions, the Prosecution should be expected to be -- fully challenge that evidence in the same amount of time. Your Honour, let's put it differently. If, prior to today, we had formally -- I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if prior to today we had formally varied our witness list and sought to cut down the amount of time we needed with this witness, it would be completely expected and natural, in my respectful submission, that Your Honours would have given a consequential order which should have reduced the time available for cross-examination to the other Defence teams and also to the Prosecution. Your Honour, we are reviewing our witness list, and it may well be the case that in times ahead, we may well try to cut down the amount of time we need with certain witnesses. I can't give any undertaking in relation to that at this moment, but we are certainly endeavouring to do that. We don't want this trial to drag on indefinitely. But in relation to this matter, it is my primary submission that one hour and fifteen minutes has been taken by lead counsel for Mr. Stojic in this case, consistent with the whole spirit underlying your decisions on the allocations of time, the Prosecution should be given one hour and fifteen minutes for cross-examination. Now, Your Honours, if, as an accomplished advocate, some tailoring needs to be done by the opposing party, that's quite usual. It's quite common place to an advocate and it can be done on one's feet, but if any prejudice is occasioned, I would invite Your Honours that we can take an early break, my learned friend can be given the 20 minutes, and in that break she can decide again what are the areas she wishes to focus on in one hour and fifteen minutes to test the credibility of the witness that has been called on behalf of Mr. Stojic. Your Honour, unless I can assist you further, those are my submissions on this matter, but I would ask that cross-examination be limited to the amount of time used by the Defence for Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stringer. I was just standing to my feet to say that the Petkovic Defence supports what's said by Mr. Khan, and, Your Honours, to regard the time provisionally allocated to the Prosecution as rigid is contrary both to the underlying rationale of Your Honour's directions, and also to what's an important element of all the directions been given that Your Honours have assured all of us and assured Your Honours yourselves throughout this trial that these guide-lines were to be applied with flexible according to the circumstances. And inflex --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Stewart please speak up for the translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's the first time in my life I've been asked to do that, but I certainly will. To apply the guide-line without that flexibility in this particular case is contrary to the underlying rationale and, in the end, will be wasteful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may also be heard on the part of the Defence. I support the previous submissions, but I should also wish to bring to everyone's attention, especially the Trial Chamber's attention, that in the past, whenever the Defence has gone beyond the stated time limitations, the Prosecution has always demanded -- demanded, and I underscore that word "demanded," that their time also be increased. So now that the Defence is taking less time because they've streamlined the direct examination, they've perhaps cut some portions of it to save time, for whatever reason, means that now the Prosecution's time should also be limited. So I think this is in keeping with the spirit and letter of your previous rulings, and I think we cannot have inconsistent standards, one applied to the Prosecution and one applied to the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Then Mr. Coric's -- MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm going to say just a couple of sentences. The first one is that I agree with everything that my colleagues have said, and the second one is that I do recall that on several occasions, when the Prosecutor completed his examination of the witness earlier than provided for on the list, the Presiding Judge said the Prosecution used this amount of time, so the Defence has this amount of time, always awarding the same time to the Defence as the Prosecution used, unless there was special permission for the Defence to get more time, but that always had to be specially approved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, Your Honour, I'd just like to say that I completely stand by my colleague and the arguments that he has put forward. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, you may intervene. Then we'll have a break, and we'll issue our decision. Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and I appreciate the opportunity to address this issue, because it obviously could relate to subsequent witnesses as well. It's interesting that this has only happened for the first time today, despite our having been in Defence cases for -- and through with Defence witnesses for many months. I don't think it's necessary for the Trial Chamber at this moment to issue a broad, definitive ruling as to what's going to happen every time that a direct examination ends earlier than was previewed. We spent a lot of time and a lot of writing on hypothetical or abstract issues. My suggestion is that since this is a new issue, let's think about it, without making any across-the-board rulings, and, most importantly, let's see whether the Prosecution needs more than an hour and fifteen minutes to cross-examine this witness. If that turns out to be the case, we'll ask for more time and the Trial Chamber can issue a ruling. It might -- as my colleague Ms. Moe has already said, it might turn out that we don't need the entire two hours, and so let's just be flexible. Let's consider this witness and the Prosecution's needs today, rather than engaging in a broader debate that might turn out to be completely moot. So that's my suggestion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I, of course, as always, listen most attentively to what my learned friend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Khan, you know that we don't like to have rebuttals, and this is already a response to a reply, and that can go on forever, because then Mr. Stewart is going to want to speak because in the meantime he may have thought of some things, same for Mr. Karnavas, and here we go again, so this can be Wimbledon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not a serve and volleyer, but it was our application, my objection. Normally the opposing party can respond, and I'm simply being asked an opportunity to reply. There has been a response by Ms. Moe, and of course then by Mr. Stringer. And so I think it's fair, as it is my objection, I have the last word. Your Honour, this matter can be dealt with summarily. Of course, the Prosecution have significant resources, and of course it will not prejudice them that much to engage in a tennis match of filing of motions, but this is a very straightforward issue which is predicated on the existing jurisprudence of Your Honours, of Your Honours. I don't think it, as a matter of principle, is appropriate to say -- to say, well, let's see if the Prosecution need to use the time, and if not it is moot. I think it's right to set, at the outset, what is the time allocated by the Prosecution. Now, Your Honours, the one hour fifteen minutes is a ceiling, it is a limit, it is not a floor. Of course, if the Prosecution wish to sit down after 15 minutes, that's their prerogative, but it's only right and proper that before standing up and conducting a cross-examination, the Prosecution should know the order of the Trial Chamber, and the Defence should know exactly how much cross-examination time the party is being given. Your Honour, as I said before, this issue is -- and my submission on this issue is completely based upon the jurisprudence and the logic behind Your Honours' previous findings and rulings. But it's quite often the case that parties say they need five hours to cross-examine a -- to examine a witness, and Your Honours say, no, two hours is appropriate. As a matter of logic, the converse also should follow. Your Honours have seen the scope of examination-in-chief, and I would ask that one hour fifteen minutes be ordered as the appropriate time given to the Prosecution to cross-examine, and the matter can be dealt with by way of an extemporaneous oral decision without a delay in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have a 20-minute break, and we'll issue our ruling after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will hand down its oral decision. The Trial Chamber would like to remind all and every one that the Stojic Defence said that since they had had an hour and a quarter, they wanted the OTP to have the same amount of time. As a follow-up to this, other Defence counsel supported Ms. Nozica's request. The Prosecutor replied and stated that he wanted to be allotted the time that had been initially allocated, i.e., two hours, whilst stating that if need be, the OTP could cut down on its time quite substantially. The Trial Chamber would like to remind all and every one that in its guide-lines, it had stipulated that the Prosecutor would have the same amount of time as what had been allocated for examination-in-chief. In this particular case, the Trial Chamber feels that in light of the examination-in-chief and in light of the questions put by other Defence counsel, that it is appropriate in this case to allocate an hour and a quarter to the Prosecutor. The Trial Chamber would also like to ask Defence counsel, in the future, if they intend to change the time allocated in the time they need, to let everybody know beforehand so that the Trial Chamber can take all appropriate decisions. The Trial Chamber would also like to ask the Prosecution, in the event that a given witness may require extra time, to seize the Chamber of this matter by providing its submissions and spelling out why this extra time is needed. Therefore, as far as this particular witness is concerned, Ms. Moe, you have an hour and a quarter. Since you have seven documents, I think you have ample time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Pinjuh. My name is Hedvig Moe.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I am a lawyer with the Prosecution, and I will be asking you some questions. I'd first like to you look up one of the documents in the binder that you discussed with Ms. Nozica, and that would be the binder that you've already looked at, the bigger one, and it's number 2D01185. 2D01185.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's the first document in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: You've found it, Mr. Pinjuh?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: That document you already discussed with Ms. Nozica, and it is a document signed by Bruno Stojic. It's from the Defence Department. And we see, up in the left-hand corner, that it's dated December 5th, 1992, in Mostar, and to the attention of Mr. Slavko Zelic, and it regards -- considers the appointment of Mr. Zelic to the commander of the brigade that you were with at the time. And this document, did I understand you correctly that it was received at the Kralj Tvrtko Brigade at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, you understood me correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And would the document have been received at the brigade on or around or right after the date that it was written or sent off, being December 5th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: You're probably right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: How was it received? How was it sent and received at the brigade? We can see, as I said, that it was signed by Mr. Stojic, and I wonder what means of communication that was used. Was it fax, was it regular mail?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: I think somebody brought it to Sarajevo, but I'm not sure who.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So you are saying you think it was delivered by hand, by a person?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you. Another document that you also looked at with Ms. Nozica, and that has number 2D01777. Sorry, 2D01177. Do you have the document, Mr. Pinjuh?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: As I mentioned, you talked to Ms. Nozica about this one as well. This is -- this goes to appointments to the Command of the brigade that you were with, and you are mentioned as number 1, "deputy commander," I think it should be; is that correct? And we see up again on the left-hand side, that it's dated December 29th, 1992, in Mostar, and we can see on page 2 of the document that again it's a document signed by Mr. Bruno Stojic. And next to his signature, we can see that it says that it's to be delivered to the Command of the Brigade of Kralj Tvrtko, as well as the HVO main headquarters and the Personnel Administration. Was this document also received at the brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: When I left Sarajevo in January, I personally picked up this document and brought it to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So it had not been sent or delivered to the brigade beforehand; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: No, no, it wasn't sent. I delivered it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And where did you -- where did you pick it up?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: The Personnel Department of the Defence Department in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And then you brought it to Sarajevo; is that correctly understood by me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So that means you picked it up at the Defence Department in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And that's where Stojic had his office; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: That was where the Defence Department was and that's where Mr. Stojic was as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you. So when you say you brought it back to the brigade, when was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Sometime towards the end of January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Was that when you came back from a trip to get resources for the HVO Brigade in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you. One more document, still in the same binder. It's number 2D01195. This is also a document that you discussed with Ms. Nozica. We see that this one is signed by Slavko Zelic, the commander of the Brigade of the Kralj Tvrtko, and we see up to -- on the left-hand corner that it's going to the main headquarters in Mostar, and it's dated February 25th, 1993, in Sarajevo. And did I understand you correctly that this document partly goes to the reason for your trip to get resources for the brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes. On the second occasion, we asked for the same resources.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Did this document arrive in Mostar at the HVO HZ-HB headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: It was protocoled, registered, so I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And where do you see that it's registered in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: I apologise. I thought it was the protocol in Mostar, but it says "Kralj Tvrtko Brigade." That's the seal. So I don't know. I wasn't in that convoy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So what you're referring to, just to clarify that, that's the stamp up on the right-hand side of the document, and that refers to it being sent from the Kralj Tvrtko Brigade in Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And then you might have answered it already, but just to get a clear reply again: Was this document received in Mostar at the HVO headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: I assume that it was, because the people who took this document arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "the people who took this document"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Well, I can see here that Damjan Moro, a commander of the brigade military police, left with this, and I met him in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So where it does say that Moro left with this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that I met him, I met Moro, who had left Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So am I understanding you correctly that you knew Moro was going on this convoy, you met him, and you think that he brought the document with him from Sarajevo? Am I understanding you correctly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Reading his name here, then I assume that it could have been done by him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly be asked to speak up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'll move on to another document, Witness, and this is in the little blue binder that you just got, the one on your right-hand side. So in the little blue binder, it's number 2D00996. And I'm being asked by the people assisting us here that, Mr. Pinjuh, you please speak into the microphone so they can hear you for the interpretation. This is a document that you can see, on the first page in the B/C/S version and on the second page in the English version, is signed by Bruno Stojic again, and on the first page we see that it's dated March the 1st, 1993. It's just one page in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: [In English] Number?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: It's 2D00996. You first have the English version, and behind the English version is the B/C/S version of the document. Do you have it there, Mr. Pinjuh?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you. As I said, we can see that it's signed by Mr. Bruno Stojic, and up in the left-hand corner we see it's dated the 1st of March, 1993. And towards the end of the document, we can see that it's going to the HVO main headquarters and to the Command of the Kralj Tvrtko Brigade. Can you see that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Did you receive this document at the brigade in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: I can't answer that with any certainty, but I think that we ought to have received this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Why do you think you ought to have received this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Because the document indicates how mobilisation should be developed of the brigade, and organised.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So this is information that you assume that the brigade had, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: I assume that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And can you say anything about how you assume the document made it to Sarajevo from Mostar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: I assume somebody brought it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So if you look just above, where it says that it's going to be sent to the main headquarters and to the Command of the Kralj Tvrtko Brigade, it says: "Summary from amendments of the mobilisation development to be delivered to:" Can you see that? And is that the reason why you think it was -- it was brought by a person to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Well, if it arrived in the Personnel Administration of the brigade, then I assume somebody brought it there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. A document that goes to a bit of a different issue. We're still in the little binder that you have in front of you, and it's number 2D01196. It's a bit further to the back. It's the last document, it should be. 2D01196. Do you have the document, Witness?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And this is, as we can see from the date on the left-hand corner, it's from 7th of November, 1993, and it says : "To the attention of the HVO Main Staff Mostar." That's to the right, the right-hand corner, and to the Citluk Forward Command Post. And if you go look at the -- to the end of the document, it is signed by Colonel Ivica Rajic. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And Ivica Rajic, he was with the HVO, was he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: In Kiseljak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: In Kiseljak, right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: If you go to point or number 2 in the document, that refers to Sarajevo, and it goes to, it says in that paragraph after Sarajevo, it says: "According to the information we have, the Croats in Sarajevo, that is, Kralj Tvrtko Brigade, has been disarmed ..." And it goes on about that same topic. What I want to ask you about, though, is the last sentence of that paragraph, and it says: "We will obtain more information about the events in Sarajevo from the XY side and forward it to you." The XY side, that's the Serbs, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer. We didn't hear him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: You will have to repeat your answer, Witness, because the interpreters didn't hear you, so we didn't get any interpretation. So could you please repeat what you said to my last question, which was whether -- or I said: The XY side, that was the Serbs, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: You don't know. You've never seen references to the XY side in any HVO documents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So when it says here -- it refers to these events in November 1993. We can agree on that, can't we, that you've been also talking about the 6th of November, 1993 disarmament of the Kralj Tvrtko Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And then Rajic says: "We will obtain more information about the event in Sarajevo..." And do you also agree with me that that should be the same event, what happened on the 6th of November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, that is the event.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: And then he says that he will obtain more information about this event that happened from the XY side. Who is the XY side?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The question is asked and answered, Your Honours. This is my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the question was asked already.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I wanted to, Mr. President, if I may, I wanted to ask the witness in the context of the actual document here, to see if we could get closer to an answer to what the XY side reference might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Context is absolutely the same. In the first instance, the paragraph of the document was read and the question was put and answered, and now again the same story, asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours, my question was: Is the XY side a reference to the Serbs. The witness said he didn't know. I'd like to ask him an open question to try and find out if we can establish who the XY side was. So I'm trying to get that question answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At this point, Your Honour, it calls for speculation. Now we're asking the witness to speculate. If the witness doesn't know, he doesn't know. You have to move on. She has to accept the answer and move on, as opposed to trying to pose 50 questions, try to guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Prosecutor, the witness said he didn't know, and I myself, I wondered -- I wonder who this XY side was. One could think they were the Serbs, but the witness said he didn't know. So please continue. We've heard other witnesses. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Let me ask you a different question, then, Witness. Did the HVO and the Serbs in Sarajevo share information with each other while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, when she says "Serbs," what does she mean by "Serbs"? Are we talking about residents of Sarajevo, are we talking about some military unit? What is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Let me rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Did the HVO and the VRS in Sarajevo share information with each other?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At which point in time are we speaking of? When was the VRS operating in Sarajevo, especially when Sarajevo was under siege? I mean, in some cases, the Prosecution is prosecuting the VRS commanders for the siege of Sarajevo. Now are we to assume that there was a unit of VRS operating in and around Sarajevo at the time when the HVO was also working in conjunction with the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I'll rephrase again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Prosecutor, one moment. You only come occasionally to the courtroom, so you're not that familiar with the proceedings. I just wanted to inform you that basically constantly or continuously we have objections by the Defence counsel when the time-period fails to be mentioned. Sometimes it is relevant; sometimes it is not. So now that you know that, think of it when you put questions, but keep in mind at all times the issue of time. Well, we know that 1991 is not 1992, 1992 is not 1993, and 1993 is not 1994, et cetera. We know that the witness stayed in Sarajevo until 1992, that he was there early 1993, and then he left Sarajevo. So there are things he knows and things he doesn't. This date is the 7th of November, 1993. You should first ask him where he was on that date, because if he was in Zagreb, or in Paris, or London, he might not know anything. So, please, ask him where he was, and, thereafter, ask questions with a time-period to avoid objections by the Defence, which is a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The foundation for my question was meant to be the time-period that the witness was in Sarajevo, and that has been established to -- well, spring of 1992, that's when his involvement with the HVO Brigade started, and he was there until April 1993, or end of March, beginning of April, 1993. So I will refer to, then, the Serbs, by the "Serbs" I'll refer to the Serb military, let me put it that way, and I'll ask again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: While you were with the HVO Brigade of Kralj Tvrtko in Sarajevo, did you share -- did you and the Serb military share information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: What period do you mean, specifically, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: I can break it down. Let's say first from April 1992. Let's start there. April 1992 to June 1992, did the HVO Kralj Tvrtko Brigade or, excuse me, the HVO brigade or battalion that you were with, did you share information with the Serbs during that period?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: No. In that period, we did not have any contacts with the Serb Army, none whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So am I understanding you correctly that you didn't give them information and you didn't receive information from them, because there was no contact; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So that is what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Let's go to June 1992, say, to October 1992. During that time did the HVO in Sarajevo, to your knowledge, share information with the Serb military?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: I don't know that the HVO shared information with the Serb Army in June 1992, no. If you're thinking of my brigade, no, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So I'm understanding you -- am I understanding you correctly that your brigade, during that period, did not share information with the Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: In that period, we did not have a brigade. We had a battalion in the -- in Novo Sarajevo that had its assignments.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: So are you relating your answer, then, to the Novo Sarajevo Battalion, and you're saying the Novo Sarajevo Battalion did not share information with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, I was the commander of Novo Sarajevo. No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: How about the other battalions; did you hear about any of those sharing information with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: I don't believe that in the difficult position that prevailed in Sarajevo, anyone wished to share information with the Serbs. Only if ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Sir, does that mean you didn't know about any sharing of information with the Serbs during that period?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: I certainly didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: My last question was related to up until October 1992. We know you stayed there until end of March, beginning of April -- I don't appreciate the comments coming from the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite right. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Going back to where I was: We stopped at October 1992 with my last question, and you were there until March/April 1993. Was there ever a time that you know about sharing of information between the Serbs and the Croats, and then I'm speaking about the military forces that were stationed there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: All I knew was the humanitarian route in the area of Stup, to leave that area leading to Kiseljak, and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Just one clarification. Am I right in understanding, from your examination or the examination by Ms. Nozica, that you were not in Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a follow-up question on this document. Witness, we know that you were not in Sarajevo in November, that we know, but this is quite a striking document in many a way. I'd like to hear your view, as a former battalion commander. This Colonel, Ivica Rajic, is writing to the headquarters on the 7th of November to address the issue of Vares, that of civilians and soldiers in Vares, and I'm amazed because he seems to be interested in the situation in Sarajevo. He is in Kiseljak, and from there he learned - we don't know how - he learned that the Tvrtko Brigade was disarmed, that there is a new commander, and so forth, and it appears that he's requesting from the headquarters to seek information on the events in Sarajevo, so it seems, by asking the XY side. So he is in Kiseljak. He's interested in what's happening in Sarajevo, but I suppose he has other tasks to deal with. Do you have an explanation or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I can understand, in Kiseljak there were refugees from Sarajevo. They had their office in Kiseljak, and probably when these things were happening, those families asked for someone to give them information about what was happening in Sarajevo, what was happening in general. I assume that that would be the only reason for something like that, because that is not in his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So your explanation is that on account of the situation in Sarajevo, the brigade having been disarmed, that could some impact on the refugees going to Kiseljak; is that your explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the refugees were from Sarajevo. They were in Kiseljak, they had their office in Kiseljak, so they could have requested to find out what was going on in Sarajevo, to see what was happening to their family members in Sarajevo. These are refugees from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this could be an explanation. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, you said that in this document, it says somewhere that Ivica Rajic was asking from the Main Staff to give them information from side XY. It doesn't say anything like that. They already have information from XY and are passing that information to the Main Staff, and are asking for some completely different things from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you said has now been recorded so that we can understand better. Yes, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: One more question to this document, Mr. Pinjuh. We have established that it is from Ivica Rajic, that he signed it. And it's correct, isn't it, that the Sarajevo HVO forces, they were within the zone of responsibility for Rajic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: I think that Rajic was the commander of the brigade in Kiseljak, and Sarajevo had its own area of responsibility. I mean, not a zone, but it's a group. The military authorities or competencies were separate.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one clarification. You've been talking about the events in Sarajevo at the beginning of November 1993, but you don't have any personal knowledge of those events, do you, being out of Sarajevo at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: This is information that I heard through the media, and then later, after a considerable amount of time, from the participants who were in Sarajevo when the brigade was disarmed, but I wasn't there myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOE
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Prosecutor. You have examined all the documents you had in your folder. Ms. Nozica, do you have any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just need to have two clarifications. I think that that is quite important.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I would like to ask you to rely on the electronic -- on e-court. You are going to get document 2D996 in e-court. This is a document, the development of mobilisation of the armed forces. The Prosecutor asked you if that reads "Sarajevo." You said you didn't know. But I would like to ask, kindly, to tell us if there is any information here, such as the code of the unit of you -- that you had and that you knew of in the time that this document was drafted?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: The code referred to here is the one that is mentioned here. I don't know exactly what our brigade code was. I guess it was this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was the brigade supposed to have a code?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: Well, if it's something that a higher instance sought, then it should have had one.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at document, in reference to His Honour Judge Trechsel's question. I would like to go back to that. During the question by my learned friend Ms. Alaburic as to what was going on in Sarajevo of the 8th of November, was it an attack, could it be considered an attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So I would like to ask you, in my binder, to look at document 2D1188. I think that that is the seventh document. Witness, the third sentence says this was a document that we saw --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes we don't have any of the documents that Ms. Nozica is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: -- when did the attack happen, and you responded to something about that. The document says all the guards have been disarmed, as well as the units holding the line of responsibility and the HVO Command arrested.
