The special units, first of all, of the corps were entrusted with the task in facilities of the HVO, left visible traces of vandalism. They were -- members of the HVO were physically mistreated. Some individuals had pistol barrels pushed into their mouths deliberately. Metal Croatian and religious insignia were put into the mouths of others for them to swallow. They trampled Croatian flags, destroyed communications equipment, smashed the doors, robbed the treasury. Food was stolen or destroyed. Is this sufficient? Witness, did you hear that this is what was going on on that day? This is how this attack was proceeding that day on the headquarters of the Kralj Tvrtko HVO Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: I found out from the media that this aggression on the Kralj Tvrtko Brigade and the leadership of the Croatian Defence Council was conducted. Later, I heard numerous stories from those members who were actually there. These were my friends, my comrades-in-arms. After a while, I found out many of the things that were happening that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir. Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one follow-up question. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true that upon reading this document, we are amazed. We can see that the ABiH and the HVO that were side by side against the Serb forces, well, there was a rather exceptional event in November, but -- when the HVO was disarmed, but apart from that there were mistreatment of HVO soldiers, the rifle is put into their mouths, they are being beaten, there are acts of vandalism, et cetera. You told us that you had comrades-in-arms that told you that. What do you put down this blind violence to? You have fighters that fight side by side against a common enemy, and then they turn against each other and then commit all that is being stated here. Maybe there are things that are exaggerated here, but if what has been written is right, what do you put it down to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PINJUH
utterances.text: I can just make an assumption, if you wish to hear it. I, as a Croat from Sarajevo, believe that with this act, the fate of Croats in Sarajevo was sealed, and that they will feel the consequences of the fact that they moved out and of everything that after that happened in Sarajevo, as Croats or Croatian people from Sarajevo. This is my assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all you can answer, nothing but this assumption. I thank you, sir. On behalf of my colleagues and in my own name, I thank you for coming to testify as a Stojic witness in The Hague. Thank you for your contribution for truth to be established. I wish you a safe trip back home, and I wish you enjoy your retirement. The usher is going to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are not going to sit tomorrow, that's the schedule, so that we can work. The Trial Chamber has already issued 661 decisions. You can imagine the work behind it all. We've got some decisions underway. You seized the Trial Chamber constantly. There are not many of us to face this avalanche. There are four Judges and a few assistants, and we are faced by the entire OTP with all their troops, the 12 Defence counsel, plus their assistants and advisors, and people working with them. There are not even 10 of us, and there are at least 50 of you, so you can imagine the amount of work that represents, and we have to be up to the task. So we do our best, in the best available time. We do endeavour to hand down our decisions as quickly as possible, but some time-periods have to be complied with, in terms of responses. We've got to comply with that. But just remember that we have, to date, issued 661 decisions. And just a few days ago, we filed a decision on the presidential transcripts. That was really a massive amount of work. So, please, think it over when you file a motion. It has to be useful and necessary, because that's the problem we're faced with. Ms. Nozica, you have scheduled four witnesses for next week. I've looked at it very closely. It would be really desirable -- I've told you that already, but it better be said again. Mr. Cengic for the 12th of March, he better be available already on Wednesday, the 11th of March. You never know, even if you scheduled one hour, there could be a procedural issue. So with regard to Mr. Masic, no problem, Monday and Tuesday. We'll start with Mr. Bato on Wednesday, and then if we could finish Wednesday with him, we could start Mr. Sandic [as interpreted] already on Wednesday, and he could go into Thursday. So do your best, your level best.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, I am almost sure that next week we will have three witnesses, and I'm going to do my utmost. But you have confused me a little bit. I don't recognize my witnesses by what is written in the transcript, but I know who is supposed to appear next week. No problem, no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ivo Masic, Ahmet Bato, and Cengic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Cengic. Our names, Bosnian names, are very difficult. I know that. I'm going to try, on Wednesday -- the first witness is coming regularly for the proofing. After that, I'm going to try to have these other two witnesses ready for Wednesday. If we finish with the first one, we can start with the second immediately on Wednesday. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would be ever so grateful. Nothing to say, Mr. Stringer, no question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Perhaps a warning. I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm just reflecting on your remarks about the number of decisions that the Trial Chamber has issued so far in these proceedings. It's regret -- with regret that I -- I'm just going to alert the Trial Chamber to the high likelihood that the Prosecution will, today or tomorrow morning, file yet another motion with respect to the existing state of witness summaries with the witness scheduled to come on the 16th of March, Mr. Bandic. You've seen, in previous submissions, the correspondence from the Prosecution team to the Stojic team, where we identified a number of remaining witnesses, where we specified precise parts of the summaries for them and asked for further elaboration to know not just about what the witness will say, but to know more about what, in fact, the witness will say. We received somewhat of a supplemental summary for Mr. Bandic. I believe it was last week. We consider that it is not sufficient. The first inclination would be to write another letter to the Stojic Defence to see whether we can work it out, but we're really mindful, especially in light of the decision that we received from the Trial Chamber yesterday in respect of this witness, that the Trial Chamber, and rightly so, is concerned about these sorts of requests coming in late, just before the witness testifies, and the perception that the Prosecution has been dilatory, that it has not brought these issues to the attention of the Trial Chamber sooner. And so rather than engaging in what we -- our concern would be additional fruitless correspondence with the Stojic team and that would only delay our bringing this issue to the attention of the Trial Chamber, we will, today or tomorrow morning, file a submission pointing out specifically what the Prosecution regards as insufficient in respect of the existing summaries we have for Mr. Bandic. So I say that with regret. I know it's difficult for the Trial Chamber to get these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if there is a motion, we shall look into it. But would it not be better for you, Ms. Nozica, and Mr. Khan, to get together around a cup of coffee and for you to tackle the issue altogether in order to settle it? Because look, what's going to happen, you're going to file a motion, you're going to have a response by the Defence, but if you could sort it out together, that would be really much better.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wish to say that I'm very sorry that my learned friend thinks that it's a fruitless or futile correspondence. We do react. I have information that additional summaries have been made for five witnesses, and I would like to ask for a little patience from my learned friend, if he hasn't received it, I mean, it's already been sent, and if it hasn't been sent, it will be sent today or tomorrow, at the latest, and I believe that he will get all the answers today or tomorrow morning, at the latest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise. It is correct, I believe, that we have responded to all correspondence that's been addressed to us by the Prosecution. I do agree with my learned friend, Mr. Stringer, that this state of affairs is most regrettable. We have said on numerous occasions it was completely avoidable, given that we have filed our 65 summaries months ago in March of 2008. But on the eve of testimony to constantly barrage a Defence team with motions of this sort is nothing short than destabilising and disorientating, given that we have many other matters to deal with. We are forward-looking, and to constantly have to cope with the huge resource of the Prosecution on these - what I am forced to submit now - are on some occasions, at least, approaching vexatious, and even frivolous motions, is a matter of the utmost regret. Your Honours, I do invite my learned friend to address any other correspondence he wishes to us, and as the state of the record discloses, we will try, in good faith, to respond. But sometimes one party or the other - it may apply to both the Prosecution and Defence - want more and more and more. Now, this does not make it correct or make it meritorious. Your Honours, I do give my learned friend now notice that once I receive his hopefully informal correspondence, I intend to -- or we intend to file, on behalf of Mr. Stojic, an order -- or an application or motion to the Trial Chamber which will be similar in scope to a prerogative order of prohibition, to prohibit the Prosecution to file motions of this nature, and this is -- this will be predicated upon a previous submission of Mr. Stojic that a waiver has taken place because the Prosecution did not do, in a timely fashion, that which they were expected to do, and to raise these issues at a pre-trial conference. They should now be estopped and prevented, by an order of prohibition, to file these motions at the very last opportunity, because to put it bluntly, it makes it almost impossible for a small Defence team to respond and prepare for trial in the days and weeks ahead. Now, Your Honours, we are, and it's a matter for my learned friend, if he wishes to, on this issue accept, there has been, I believe, a genuine effort on the part of the Stojic team to respond to inquiries made by the Prosecution, and I'd invite him to do that. And on previous occasions I have said, on behalf of Mr. Stojic, that unilaterally, irrespective of any motions, we are trying to supplement and give further information when we have it, and I think we have -- we have done that, in part. We have given summaries even of witnesses that the Prosecution have not requested additional information. So, Your Honour, all these matters can be decided in due course. It is a matter of regret, but as the issue has been raised by my learned friend, Mr. Stringer, quite properly, I do give the Trial Chamber notice of our intention, once we've seen his correspondence either by way of a bilateral correspondence out of court or by way of a formal motion, the choice of course being his and that of the Prosecutor. It is our intention to file a motion seeking a prohibition of the Prosecution to engage in motions which they, no doubt very sincerely, very sincerely, believe are with merit, but we say are completely without merit, are untimely, and have the effect of destabilising a small Defence team funded by legal aid, with the limitation of resources that that brings, to the extent that it is affecting the ability of the Stojic team to properly and diligently present a defence case, because it is constantly seeking to put out fires presented by the Prosecution or lit by the Prosecution on eve of testimony. This state of affairs, I emphasise as robustly as I can, was completely preventable if the Prosecution had, in a timely fashion, raised objections since March 2008, and to do so now is causing us very severe prejudice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer -- I shall give you the floor, Ms. Alaburic. Mr. Stringer, when I addressed the issue of the 661 decisions a while ago, I didn't think you were going to bring this problem up again. A few weeks ago, I told you, Mr. Stringer, and I told Mr. Scott that you needed, right away, to look at the summary list of the 65 ter witnesses, the upcoming witnesses, and say, Well, for this witness, I don't agree with this and that and that, and that is missing, to avoid this kind of situation arising. You're all professionals, you're all excellent professionals. The Trial Chamber then has to rule on these matters, and this would not occur if you were able to talk to each other, whether it's the Defence or whether it's the OTP. We understand full well. Nonetheless, you're all lawyers, and you should have the interests of justice at heart. Things have to move ahead quickly and efficiently, and we shouldn't waste our time. Rather than filing written motions, the best would be to discuss it among yourselves and only seize the Trial Chamber when you cannot find a solution. In this particular case, it seems, Mr. Stringer, that you have been too quick to respond. From what I understood, I may be mistaken, but Ms. Nozica has already prepared her replies, which she was going to put to us or give us tomorrow morning. I always listen to Mr. Khan very carefully, like I do every time Mr. Khan takes the floor. The OTP should not destabilise the Defence teams automatically. I don't know whether this is the case. This is what Mr. Khan believes, anyway. You have completed your case, the Prosecution case. It's now up to the Defence, with their limited means, to call their witnesses. There are three lawyers and three assistants perhaps, so it's a very small team. And if you swamp them with motions all the time, they won't be able to manage all of this. This you should understand. And we have to guarantee the fairness of the trial and the equality of arms. So let's wait and see what Ms. Nozica has to say, but only seize the Trial Chamber if you can't do otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If I could offer just a few brief remarks in reply, Mr. President. We took the Trial Chamber's admonition to heart last month when it directed the Prosecution to go back over the summaries. We wrote a long letter to the Defence, and we sent it to them on the 3rd of February. A copy of the letter was provided to the Trial Chamber's legal officer. Here we are now, more than a month later. We've got a little bit of supplemental information in about Mr. Bandic, but in our view it's not sufficient. We waited until we received the Stojic Defence team's exhibit list yesterday, one day late, in order to try to factor that in. We still believe that the information provided does not put us in the position we're entitled to be, in terms of knowing, not verbatim, but in general what the witness is going to say about a number of very important issues, particularly the SIS investigation at Stupni Do. We don't know what he's going to say, and that information still has not come across to us. Here we are, a month later. The Defence now are saying that we're late. Well, if we're late, it's because we've been waiting, and we've been dealing, through correspondence, with them, and yet we're still not in the position that we believe we ought to be. In light of Mr. Khan's remarks about their seeking to prohibit the Prosecution from filing motions, I don't know that we can work this out with the Stojic Defence team, and I regret to say that I think that it will be up to the Trial Chamber to have to resolve all these issues. I'm happy to meet with Mr. Khan, or Ms. Nozica, or any member of their team over coffee, but that's not going to give us the summary that we have to have in the courtroom, in the event the witness goes beyond the scope of a summary. It doesn't -- that sort of informal chat just doesn't put us in the place that we need to be when the witness is in the box and we are getting ready for a cross-examination or we are listening to a direct examination. And so I'm happy to meet with them and to raise these issues personally with them, but in light of the remarks made, we're certainly not doing this to destabilise anybody. We're just trying to be prepared, and that's all. And in our view, we're not prepared, still, in respect of Mr. Bandic, even though this was raised with the Defence team for Mr. Stojic over a month ago in the correspondence we sent to them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm always delighted to spend any time in the company of my learned friend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Khan, we will have to stop. I shall be in this courtroom in a few minutes' time, so we only have a few minutes left. Please proceed, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm most grateful. I would be more than delighted to take my learned friend up on his offer to sit down over a coffee and to discuss these issues with him, even if he's willing to accept, and I'm happy to pay for the coffee, but, Your Honours, we have responded in a timely fashion. To the best of my knowledge, the correspondence referred to by my learned friend was responded to by the Stojic Defence team on the 10th and on the 13th, so that the information given has been provided. That's the first point. The second point, Your Honour, is this: that my learned friend states that in the event of testimony going beyond the 65 ter summary, there is prejudice. Well, that is rather anticipatory. What I would rather invite Your Honours to consider is this: We have sought to endeavour to comply with our obligations under 65 ter. We have sought to supplement, wherever we can, both when the Prosecution have asked for more information and since this issue became a rather heated issue between the parties, we've looked at matters again and are working on these issues, but, Your Honour, what I would ask is that perhaps witnesses can come without what we say are needless motions by the Prosecution. After the examination-in-chief is concluded, if the Prosecution can establish or persuade Your Honours that they are really prejudiced by a matter that they were not aware of and they were not familiar of -- familiar with, at that point Your Honours can grant some time for an adjournment for them to be prepared. Your Honours, that's a very fair way of doing it. But, Your Honours, to keep flooding us with an incessant barrage of motions is destabilising. I'm saying this is a tactical device on behalf of my learned friend, Mr. Stringer. I know him too well to say that he would descend to such tactics. I'm sure that it's based upon a sincere belief that they are entitled to more and more, and of course they want statements in reality. But, Your Honours, if there is a modicum of merit -- a degree of merit in what the Prosecution say, that mischief or that prejudice could be surely remedied by the Defence after the witness has been heard, being given a few moments of time, depending upon what the issue is, to prepare, prior to conducting their cross-examination. Your Honour, that's the way of dealing with it in a fair and proper manner. Your Honour, the final remark is this: Your Honour has heard today that the witness that has concluded his evidence. It may perhaps be pertinent to note that the Prosecution filed several motions in relation to this witness, and in these motions the Prosecution's constant averment was that this witness was not relevant. And, Your Honour, all those motions, of course, we have to respond to. Now, Your Honours, you have heard the evidence today, and of course it's for Your Honours to decide if that evidence was relevant or is a complete waste of the Court's time, but the simple point is: Be that as it may, when a motion is filed by the machinery of the Office of the Prosecution, the small wheel that is available the Defence must move at a frenetic pace in order to respond and protect, to the best of our abilities, Mr. Stojic's rights to a fair trial. Your Honour, those are my remarks. I'm very happy to speak to Mr. Stringer on this issue. We're very happy to try to give as much information as we have, consistent with our obligations under the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Court. And the final remark is: Any prejudice suffered can be remedied without a constant barrage of motions by some time being given once Your Honours have seen whether or not prejudice is occasioned to a party in reality, as opposed to this theoretical spectre that is constantly being raised by, in my respectful submission, my learned friends from the Prosecution. Your Honours, those are my remarks on this issue. I hope they assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, we know that your client wished to be here when Mr. Bandic is coming. That is all right, is it; your client will be here in two weeks' time?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my client will be here precisely pursuant to your decision. He arrives on Sunday, so my client will be here when Mr. Ivan Bandic is examined, and everybody in this courtroom knows full well that we're very interested in hearing -- in having my client, General Petkovic, hear the testimony of this witness. And since Mr. Stringer raised the question, I'd like to inform the Trial Chamber of the following fact: Yesterday, we received a list of exhibits which the Defence of Bruno Stojic intends to present to Mr. Bandic and discuss the documents with Mr. Bandic. However, among those documents there are certain orders signed by my client and certain documents sent to my client, and from this we can conclude, without any doubt, that Mr. Bandic will be mentioning General Petkovic and talking about him, and I'd like to tell the Stojic Defence today that we would like to have information about the facts that the witness will be discussing and presenting relating to General Petkovic and the Main Staff in the portion which relates to General Petkovic. And I do believe that we'll be able to agree on these points with the Bruno Stojic Defence. We know the difficulties that face them. We don't want to exert any pressure on them, and it will be sufficient for us to receive the information in the course of the proofing session of Mr. Bandic. And if we receive them 24 hours prior to the examination-in-chief of the witness, we will be ready to start our cross-examination straight away. But if we don't receive that information, then we might need to ask that the proceedings be deferred, a stay in the proceedings, until we're able to prepare. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, you have just heard what Ms. Alaburic has said. You must avoid adjourning and asking the witnesses to come later. If Ms. Alaburic says she doesn't have enough information to conduct her cross-examination, this could be an issue, so please settle this among yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really will try and do the best I can. I have some technical problems, but we will respond to Ms. Alaburic's request. And if -- when it comes to time, now, when I have a proofing session, whether I can provide all the information prior -- 24 hours prior to his coming into court, I don't know. Well, they can recall the witness for the cross-examination. But as I say, I will do my best to comply. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I don't know how you prepare to hear your witnesses. The easiest would have been to ask the upcoming witness to provide you with a short summary of the items he or she wishes to discuss in light of the position he or she held at the time, so then you have a good work tool. If you wait for the last minute, then you will have a problem. So that's for you to do, that's your problem. I'm sorry to say that the Rules in this case did not enable the Bench to handle this energetically before the trial started. Unfortunately, all these problems are due to this. If all of this had been settled beforehand, we would have gained a lot of time. Unfortunately, this is not the case. It's now time to stop. I thought we would have stopped earlier, but we finish at the usual time. We shall meet again on Monday at a quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 9th day of March, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 25
